lpn.context: Hydraulic head — energy per unit weight of water, expressed as a height of water column. The ROOT concept behind head loss, velocity head, weir head, and gross/net head. A length, never a pressure. Appears as a bare label in Weir Flow (ws_headWaterHeight), Orifice (or_head), and Manning Pipe Flow (mpf_velocity_head). Acceptable English synonyms (translate the concept, not the exact word): energy elevation, hydraulic grade line (HGL).

lpn.context: Energy loss expressed as a height of water column. Appears in Darcy-Weisbach, Hazen-Williams, Manning pipe, and Penstock calculators. The English 'head' is itself jargon, and many languages express this concept in pressure terms as their professional standard — use whichever phrasing your language's hydraulic engineers actually use, and keep it consistent with the rest of that language's file.
lpn.translation_notes: 'Head' in the hydraulic sense (energy per unit weight) does not translate literally in many languages — use the established civil/hydraulic engineering phrase. Pre-2026 sr/hr human translations used 'gubitak pritiska' (= pressure loss), which is technically the same concept expressed in pressure terms rather than head terms. The current 'губитак напора / gubitak tlačne visine' (= loss of hydraulic head) is more precise in a hydraulic engineering context and is preferred. lpn.context: In lpn_, a storage node whose water level RISES AND FALLS as it fills and empties: a service reservoir, a standpipe, a clearwell, a farm storage. It is the sibling of a reservoir, which holds a level that never moves. Toolbar label lpn_tool_add_tank; the "T" ID prefix. A steady-state solve cannot tell the two apart at any one instant, which is exactly why the two need different names on screen -- the difference is in what happens NEXT.

THE THREE LEVEL FIELDS ARE DEPTHS measured up from the tank floor, not elevations on the site datum, and the English labels say "depth" for exactly that reason (Wave 0, 2026-08-14) -- do not translate them with the word your language uses for a water-surface ELEVATION. | [2026-08-14, sprint 316] Harvested from the SHIPPED strings, not from agent prose. That note had been carrying a usable tank word in 26 languages for months, waiting for the element to exist -- so when a cut feature is later built, READ THE STRING THAT ANNOUNCED IT WAS CUT before commissioning a new term.

lpn.context: In lpn_, a LINK -- it sits in the line between two nodes, like a pipe or a pump, not on a node. Five kinds are offered by what they do: a throttle valve (TCV) holding a fixed loss, a pressure reducing valve (PRV), a pressure sustaining valve (PSV) and a flow control valve (FCV). The last three open, close, or partly close by themselves as the water changes.

Supply the noun if your language needs it; the parenthesised letters are the international abbreviation and stay as written, in every script and in RTL. lpn.context: The one number that tells a valve what to do -- and it is A DIFFERENT PHYSICAL QUANTITY FOR EACH TYPE: a PRESSURE for a PRV or PSV, a FLOW for an FCV, and a dimensionless minor-loss coefficient for a TCV. The page therefore shows three different labels in the same slot (lpn_field_valve_setting_pressure / _flow / _loss) rather than one vague "Setting".
lpn.translation_notes: Seeded 2026-08-14 (ROADMAP Task 248 phase 2). The three labels are alternatives for ONE field, so keep them recognisably parallel with each other in your language, the way "Pressure setting" and "Flow setting" are parallel in English. Note that the third one, the throttle valve's loss coefficient, is the SAME KIND OF NUMBER as the pipe minor-loss coefficient k (lpn_field_km) but is a separate field and never appears beside it: a throttle valve is given no minor-loss box, because EPANET ignores one there. Translations deliberately empty; fill from the sprint output.

lpn.context: A property value that belongs to ONE scenario alone and stands in place of the Base value while that scenario is active. A scenario is nothing but a collection of these laid over the shared drawing. The status strip counts them and calls them "Own values" (lpn_scenario_overrides); the per-field checkbox that creates one is "Only in this scenario" (lpn_scenario_override).
lpn.translation_notes: Seeded 2026-08-14 (ROADMAP Task 248 / Task 184) after Wave 0 found the eigenvalue collision in the English label "Own values". The concept a translator wants is the one scenario managers in InfoWater/WaterGEMS use: a value CHANGED IN THIS CASE ONLY. It must read naturally in a very narrow status strip beside the units readout, followed by a count ("Own values: 3"). Note the suite ALREADY uses "local" as a technical term -- "Minor (local) loss" -- so a rendering built on the word "local" collides with an established meaning on the same page and should be avoided. Translations deliberately empty; fill from the sprint output. | [2026-08-14, sprint 316] Harvested from the SHIPPED strings, not from agent prose. THE ENGLISH MOVED BECAUSE OF WHAT THIS SPRINT MEASURED: lpn_scenario_overrides is now 'Custom values', not 'Own values' (Tom: "I love 'custom'. 'Changed' is a little dangerous"). TEN languages independently detected and routed around the eigenvalue calque -- es pt cs it ro uk bg sr de hr -- far wider than the three Wave 0 predicted, and six hit it a second time in lpn_scenario_push_none, a key Wave 0 never flagged. 'Custom' has no calque path into mathematics in any of them, so the trap stops existing rather than being dodged 26 times. THE SECOND FINDING IS THE MORE USEFUL ONE. Clustering the renderings by MEANING split them three ways: 'its own' (13), 'custom/specific/exclusive' (7) and 'CHANGED' (cs hr bg). The third is FALSE here -- a scenario's custom value may be identical to Base's, which scenario-harness.js asserts outright -- and it was invisible in any single language. Being forced off a calque makes a translator CHOOSE a reading, so a divergence in those forced choices measures how many readings the English has. All three were corrected: cs Specificke, hr Svoje, bg Svoi, de Individuelle. ON THE hr/sr APPARENT CONTRADICTION, settled rather than split: 'vlastita vrijednost' IS a documented alternate name for eigenvalue in CROATIAN, while Serbian's dominant term uses a different root (sopstvena), so 'vlastite' is safe in sr and not in hr. Two closely related languages, two genuinely different answers -- do not harmonise them.

lpn.context: The part of a program that computes the answer. In lpn_ there are TWO of them and the UI contrasts them in one sentence: EPANET's own solver, and this suite's built-in solver. Both must be recognisable as the same KIND of thing and distinguishable from each other, so use one noun for both and let the qualifier (EPANET vs built-in) carry the difference.
lpn.translation_notes: [2026-08-13, sprint 252] English was "engine" until Tom changed it to "solver" suite-wide. The evidence that the ENGLISH was the defect, not the translations: 20+ languages were already internally inconsistent, using a correct solver word for the BUILT-IN solver and a motor word for EPANET's -- in the same sentence. sr језгро vs решавач; cs výpočetní jádro vs řešič; id mesin vs penyelesai; hi इंजन vs सॉल्वर; tr motor vs çözücü; ro motorul vs rezolvitorul. Every agent independently resolved it toward the solver word it already had. Russian had avoided the trap from the start (расчётное ядро) and Chinese noted 引擎 unambiguously means a physical engine, so there was no trade-off to make there. Values below are harvested from the shipped lpn_engine_loading strings and verified present in them (bg/ru/uk appear in inflected case).

lpn.context: A drawing of ground elevation and hydraulic grade against distance along a chosen route through the network -- what a civil engineer calls a profile or a long section, as opposed to the plan view the map shows. Use the surveying / civil drawing term of the language, the one that names the sheet a designer reads pipe grades off.
lpn.translation_notes: [2026-08-19, sprint 438 wave 0] Raised as the highest-traffic string of the profile feature: lpn_profile_menu is one word and names the menu, so a wrong choice mislabels everything under it. English is kept because it is the engineering term of art; the guard belongs here.

lpn.context: The line joining the elevations to which water would rise in open tubes along the pipe: elevation head plus pressure head. Drawn against the ground line on a profile, and the quantity a designer checks minimum pressure against.
lpn.translation_notes: [2026-08-19, sprint 438 wave 0] The chart legend key lpn_profile_hgl and the prose in lpn_profile_tip must come out as the SAME phrase; they were diverging in English ("Hydraulic grade" vs "hydraulic grade line") and the English has been made to agree. The existing "energy grade line" entry is the neighbouring concept and should use a parallel construction.

lpn.context: EPANET's time series of multipliers: the base demand at a junction is multiplied by the pattern value for the current time step. A pattern belongs to the file and has a name; several junctions may share one.
lpn.translation_notes: [2026-08-19, sprint 438 wave 0] The word carries the .inp import report (lpn_inp_drop_patterns, lpn_inp_drop_demand_pattern) and the clock, so one rendering must serve all of them.

lpn.context: IMGD is imperial million gallons per day, MGD is US million gallons per day. Both appear in the same flow-unit selector, one row apart.
lpn.translation_notes: [2026-08-19, sprint 438 wave 0] Raised because the two tokens sit together and neither says which gallon it uses. The user-facing confusability is a separate question for Tom; the translator instruction is simply to leave both tokens alone.

lpn.context: EPANET's pressure breaker valve: it forces a fixed pressure drop between its two ends, in the direction of flow, whatever the flow is. Its siblings in the same selector are PRV, PSV, FCV, TCV and GPV.
lpn.translation_notes: [2026-08-19, sprint 438 wave 0] English kept: it is EPANET's published element name and identity terms are not renamed. Where the language's water field has no settled phrase, a descriptive rendering ("valve that drops the pressure by a fixed amount") beats reaching for the electrical word.

lpn.context: A project is in one of two modes. A lat/lon project has geographic coordinates and can draw a street map behind it; an XY project is drawn on a plain local grid with no place on the Earth. The names appear in lpn_geomap, lpn_xymap and in the prose of lpn_georef_menu, lpn_georef_tip, lpn_georef_intro, lpn_georef_confirm, lpn_georef_done, lpn_georef_on_map and the four New project rows.
lpn.translation_notes: [2026-08-19, sprint 438 wave 0] Raised because the names are coined and nothing marked them as coined, so some agents would translate them and others keep them. A per-label synonym would have to be repeated across nine strings; one concept pointer is the right shape.

lpn.context: Which edge or centre of a text label lines up with its anchor point: horizontal alignment left / centre / right, vertical alignment top / middle / bottom. Use the word a word processor or drawing program in the language uses for that control.
lpn.translation_notes: [2026-08-19, sprint 438 wave 0] The English was wrong and has been fixed (justification -> alignment) in lpn_field_text_align and lpn_field_text_valign. Keep the two labels parallel: one word for both axes.

lpn.context: To leave a value or a whole label off the map because there is not enough room to print it. The Labels box has a column headed with this word (lpn_labels_col_drop), holding a number that orders which value or which test is given up first; the term of art, Priority, lives in that heading's tip. Use the word your language would use for leaving something out of a drawing for want of space.
lpn.translation_notes: [2026-08-19, sprint 438 Wave 0] The heading replaced an icon and sits in a column about three characters wide, so it must stay very short -- but shortness is exactly what makes the polysemy dangerous: on a hydraulics page a bare "drop" reads first as a drop in head or elevation. Keep it short AND unmistakably about leaving a label off.

lpn.context: One computation of the network over its whole time period: every reporting time from the first to the last, one after another. The button lpn_time_run carries the word alone and must be an IMPERATIVE VERB addressed to the user ("compute it now"); the surrounding strings use the same word as a NOUN ("the start of the run"). Where your language needs different words for the two, use each in its place, and keep the noun consistent across lpn_time_run_tip, lpn_time_run_note and lpn_time_duration.
lpn.translation_notes: [2026-08-19, sprint 438 Wave 0] EPANET calls this a run, and lpn_time_run_note quotes the button label inside a sentence -- so the word chosen for the button must be the word that appears in that sentence, or the instruction points at a button that is not there.

lpn.context: This suite's plain-English verb for "compute" or "solve": to calculate the flows, pressures and heads of the network. Chosen over "calculate" and "solve" because it is Simple English, and it recurs across the clock strings (lpn_time_run_tip, lpn_time_run_note, lpn_time_running, lpn_time_no_engine). Use your language's ordinary verb for calculating a result -- there is no need for an idiom, and no need to copy the two-word English shape.
lpn.translation_notes: [2026-08-19, sprint 438 Wave 0] Raised because the phrasal verb is opaque word by word: a reader who parses "work" plus "out" gets exercise, not arithmetic. One rendering should serve all four strings.

lpn.context: The mark between the whole and fractional parts of a number: a dot in English (17.5), a comma in most of Europe, Latin America and elsewhere (17,5). Numbers that appear INSIDE a translated string as EXAMPLES carry the locale's own separator -- write 17,5 where your language writes 17,5. The page accepts both when the user types (js/lpn-patterns.js takes <digits>,<digits> as a decimal), so an example with a comma is a working example, not a broken one. Affects lpn_time_format_tip and lpn_labels_col_decimals_example.
lpn.translation_notes: [2026-08-19, sprint 438 Wave 0] Precedent set for lpn_labels_col_decimals_example, whose whole value is the example 0.000 and which Tom said may become 0,000 where needed. lpn_time_format_tip carries four such examples and nothing in the English says they are localisable.

keys_to_translate.lpn_library_controls_tip: A control is one sentence that opens or closes a link, or gives it a setting, when a water level, a pressure or a time says so.

keys_to_translate.lpn_library_default_pattern_tip: Every junction with no pattern uses this one.
